title: Training in Toilet Use and Self-Reliance
summary: This lesson addresses "training in toilet use and self-reliance" for children from two to three years old. Teach him istinja’ (cleansing after relieving oneself) and its importance, and train him to enter the bathroom with the left foot and exit with the right, while memorizing the du’a (supplication) for entering and exiting to instill these manners as part of his routine. It is advised to begin when the child shows readiness (typically between the ages of two and three). Starting too early before readiness may cause stress and setbacks that prolong the training period. Guide him gently to serve himself and prepare his own needs; this will accustom him early to diligence and self-reliance, protecting him from indulgence and dependency.
try_this: Try this week: Teach him istinja’ and its importance, train him to enter the bathroom with the left foot and exit with the right, and help him memorize the du’a for entering and exiting to instill these good manners as part of his routine.
reflection_prompts: How can I begin teaching my child the proper manners for using the toilet (relieving himself)?
When is the best time to start training my child to use the toilet to avoid frustrating him?

review_defects.why: The Arabic uses 'الآداب' (al-adab, meaning manners/etiquette), not 'الأخلاق' (al-akhlaq, meaning morals/character). Transliterating it as 'akhlaq' introduces a different Islamic concept. The correct transliteration is 'adab' or the translation 'manners'.

review_defects.english: Teach him ... train him ... Guide him
review_defects.why: The Arabic uses feminine singular imperatives directly addressing the mother, creating a warm, personal tone. The English uses neutral imperatives without 'your child' or 'you', making it impersonal and less direct.

review_defects.english: while memorizing the du’a (supplication) for entering and exiting
review_defects.why: The Arabic presents memorization as a separate action (noun) in a list of three instructions. The English turns it into a participial phrase ('while memorizing'), implying it happens simultaneously with the entering/exiting training, which is not stated in the Arabic.

review_defects.english: and help him memorize the du’a for entering and exiting
review_defects.why: The Arabic simply says 'and memorization of the du’a' without specifying who helps. The English adds 'help him', inserting an agent not present in the source.
